In Scandinavian folklore, the marsh Labrador tea
plant, a flowering shrub that grows abundantly in northern
regions, have been esteemed as a convenient and natural
moth repellant. Since the medieval era, people have
stored the shrub’s evergreen branches with winter
clothing in an effort to deter wool-gnawing moths. The
practice of storing the branches with winter clothing
remains popular today. However, reasons for its success
have been largely speculative—that is, until recently,
when scientists inadvertently uncovered an explanation.
